newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco deal possible this week - sources.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco deal possible this week - sources.

text.p: State attorneys general are optimistic they can present the White House with a tobacco settlement proposal this week, although some problem areas such as punitive damages may be unresolved, sources close to the talks said Monday.

Two key negotiators, Mississippi Attorney General Mike Moore and plaintiffs lawyer Dick Scruggs, met with White House staff members early Monday afternoon to provide an update on the talks. The two men met with tobacco industry representatives earlier Monday.
Sources said some negotiators hope to have a proposal to the White House as soon as Tuesday or Wednesday.
Moore would not comment on when a proposal might be finished. However, he told Reuters "things are going real well. We're gonna get there."
A large group of attorneys general were involved in a meeting Monday afternoon to discuss various issues, including language in a settlement that would make it binding in each of their states.
A news briefing was set for later Monday.

The attorneys general, the highest ranking legal officers of each state, and the tobacco industry have been negotiating since early April. Mississippi's Moore has been trying to reach a deal prior to his state's Medicaid trial against the industry, set to begin July 7.

Moore was the first of 37 attorneys general to sue the tobacco industry to recoup Medicaid health care costs of treating smokers. As recently as Thursday, California, the largest state, joined the battle by seeking to recover some $433 million it estimates it spends each year on sick smokers.

As the talks continued in Washington, the legal battle against the tobacco industry was set to spread to Canada. On Monday, British Columbia announced legislation paving the way for the province to become the first in Canada to sue tobacco companies to recoup medical costs for treating smokers.

The province is believed to be the first government outside the United States to pursue such action against tobacco manufacturers. Several other Canadian provinces and the Canadian federal government are considering following suit, officials said.

"The legal battle against the tobacco industry is spreading as governments not only in the United States but worldwide believe this is a battle that should be fought and won," said British Columbia Health Minister Joy MacPhail.
Before British Columbia files its lawsuit, the government said it was first asking the tobacco industry to compensate it voluntarily for tobacco-related illness and smoking prevention programmes.

Under the terms discussed so far in the talks in Washington, the industry would set up a fund to pay for awards in individual lawsuits. A final figure has not been decided, but there would be an annual ceiling so the industry would know about how much it would have to pay each year.
In the health area, the industry has agreed to sharp limits on cigarette advertising, including a ban on the use of cartoon characters and human figures.

The industry has agreed to penalties if smoking by youngsters fails to fall 30 percent in five years and 60 percent in 10. Penalties would be based on how much the industry can earn from a teenage smoker over his or her life.

Cigarette package warnings would also be strengthened to include language such as "cigarettes are addictive and can cause fatal lung disease in non-smokers." The warnings will be increased in size and placed on the front of packages.
The industry has also agreed to fund smoking cessation programmes and devices for those who cannot afford them.
